title: Catholic: works of mercy
hookLine: feed the hungry, visit the sick, welcome the stranger (Matthew 25:35–36)
last: THE HAIL MARY — FULL OF GRACE.

cards: In one of Jesus' stories, every nation stands before a king on his throne. People are sorted to his right and his left, about to learn what the whole trial was about. The questions ought to be enormous.
What did you believe? What did you achieve? Instead the king talks about a plate of food, a visit to someone sick, a spare coat.
And everyone, on both sides, is surprised. Today: the story behind the works of mercy.

teach.b: Jesus tells of the Son of Man coming in glory to judge the nations, and the king says to those on his right, in the Douay-Rheims translation: "For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink; I was a stranger, and you took me in."
Naked, and you clothed me; sick, and you visited me; in prison, and you came to me. They're confused.

teach.h: WHEN DID WE SEE YOU HUNGRY?
teach.b: When did we ever see you hungry? And the king answers: "Amen I say to you, as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." That's the surprise.
Nobody on either side knew they'd met him. He was the hungry person. The stranger.
Out of this passage the Catholic Church drew a list: the seven corporal works of mercy, corporal meaning of the body. Feed the hungry. Give drink to the thirsty.
Clothe the naked. Shelter the homeless. Visit the sick.
Visit the imprisoned. Bury the dead, that last one taken from the book of Tobit.
Alongside them sit seven spiritual works of mercy, for the heart and mind: among them, comfort the sorrowful, forgive offenses, bear wrongs patiently, and pray for the living and the dead.
Catholic teaching presents these not as extras for especially holy people, but as the everyday shape of faith: a meal, a visit, a coat, a word of comfort.

how: Catholic parishes run food pantries, hospital and prison visits and funeral ministries as works of mercy, and many Catholics choose one work of mercy as a practice, especially during Lent.

practice: Go through the list slowly in your mind: hungry, thirsty, without clothes or a home, sick, in prison, grieving. Who near you fits one of them: a coworker who skips lunch, a friend in the hospital, a neighbor who's lonely?
Choose one person and one work, and picture yourself doing it.
